nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the time play, the condition-of-England essay and the popular theatre
literary_identity: Novelist, dramatist and essayist; the great middlebrow man of letters of the period, the author of Dangerous Corner, Time and the Conways and The Good Companions.
biography: Born John Boynton Priestley at Bradford on 13 September 1894; he served in the infantry from 1914 and was wounded and gassed, took his degree at Cambridge after the war, and made his name with The Good Companions (1929) and Angel Pavement (1930). He wrote some fifty plays — Dangerous Corner (1932), Laburnum Grove (1933), Time and the Conways (1937), When We Are Married (1938), An Inspector Calls (1945) — and broadcast and wrote on English social questions for forty years. He died at Stratford-upon-Avon on 14 August 1984.
literary_profile: Priestley invented the modern English time play and brought the condition-of-England argument to the commercial stage: Dangerous Corner and Time and the Conways are the finest technical experiments in the interwar theatre, An Inspector Calls is the most performed English play after the war, and The Good Companions is the period's most popular English novel. His broadcasts of 1940–41 made him a national figure and nearly cost him his wartime career.
stylistic_characteristics: The symmetrical three-act play with a single set and a small cast; the time-slip that reveals the present from the future (Time and the Conways); the detective structure used as social argument (An Inspector Calls); the comic picaresque of the English road (The Good Companions); the plain essayistic prose of the broadcast.
intellectual_concerns: The English class system and the condition of England; time, determinism and the possibility of change; the provincial town and the touring company; the First World War and the lost generation; money, business and the moral compromise; the ordinary English life.
historical_significance: Priestley invented the modern English time play, wrote the most popular English novel of the period in The Good Companions, and made the condition-of-England argument a form of popular theatre in An Inspector Calls. His wartime broadcasts made him the period's most trusted public voice.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the well-made play, the restraint of feeling and the English middle-class drama
literary_identity: Dramatist; the finest English writer of the well-made play, the author of The Winslow Boy, The Browning Version and Separate Tables.
biography: Born Terence Mervyn Rattigan in London on 10 June 1911; he read at Trinity College, Oxford, and made his name with French Without Tears (1936), After the Dance (1939), The Winslow Boy (1946), The Browning Version (1948), The Deep Blue Sea (1952) and Separate Tables (1954). The arrival of Look Back in Anger in 1956 made him unfashionable for a decade; he was reassessed before his death at Hamilton, Bermuda, on 30 November 1977, and his centenary in 2011 restored him to the centre of the English theatre.
literary_profile: Rattigan is the finest English writer of the well-made play: The Winslow Boy, The Browning Version and Separate Tables are the most accomplished plays in the English language of their kind, and their restraint — the emotion held under the surface of the dialogue — is a technique the English theatre has never excelled. He wrote the period's great plays about the price of respectability, and the reaction against him in 1956 is one of the period's revealing literary scandals.
stylistic_characteristics: The tight three-act construction with a single set and a small cast; the dialogue that never states the feeling; the understated curtain line; the public-school and the service officer as material; the social comedy that becomes a tragedy without a change of tone.
intellectual_concerns: The English middle class and its code of restraint; respectability and its price; the law, the newspaper and the ruined reputation (The Winslow Boy); the unhappy marriage and the loveless life; the officer and the schoolmaster; homosexuality in a society that punished it.
historical_significance: Rattigan wrote the finest English well-made plays of the century: The Winslow Boy, The Browning Version and Separate Tables are permanent, his restraint is a technique of great sophistication, and his fall and recovery is the period's clearest example of how literary reputations are made.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the desert memoir and the prose of the Arab Revolt
literary_identity: Soldier, archaeologist and writer; the author of Seven Pillars of Wisdom, the finest English prose account of the First World War in the Middle East.
biography: Born Thomas Edward Lawrence at Tremadog, Wales, on 16 August 1888; he read history at Oxford, worked as an archaeologist at Carchemish in Syria (1911–14), and served in the Arab Bureau in Cairo and with the Arab forces under Feisal from 1916 to 1918. He wrote Seven Pillars of Wisdom (privately printed 1926, published 1935), abridged it as Revolt in the Desert (1927), and translated Homer and Forestier; he enlisted in the RAF under an assumed name, and died of injuries from a motorcycle accident at Bovington Camp, Dorset, on 19 May 1935.
literary_profile: Lawrence wrote the finest English prose account of the war in the Middle East: Seven Pillars of Wisdom is a great memoir, a study of a national revolt and the confession of a man who believed he had betrayed the cause he served. Its prose — sonorous, exact, self-lacerating — is among the finest in twentieth-century English, and it is the only soldier's book of the period to rank with Blunden's and Sassoon's.
stylistic_characteristics: The memoir written as a confession and a history at once; the exact topography of the desert; the prose that swells into the biblical and the epic; the self-examination that turns against the narrator; the ethnographic observation of the Arab tribes.
intellectual_concerns: The Arab Revolt and the making of the modern Middle East; empire, betrayal and the promises of 1916; the desert and the Arab people; the individual and the historical role; guilt, self-punishment and the divided self; the machine (the aeroplane, the motor bike) and the archaic world.
historical_significance: Lawrence wrote the finest English memoir of the First World War in the Middle East and one of the great English prose works of the century: Seven Pillars of Wisdom is a permanent classic, its account of the Arab Revolt remains the essential literary record of the making of the modern Middle East, and its self-lacerating honesty makes it unique among the war books.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the short comic story and the satire of Edwardian society
literary_identity: Short-story writer; the greatest English writer of the comic short story, the master of the surprise ending, and a satirist of Edwardian society more savage than any of his contemporaries.
biography: Born Hector Hugh Munro at Akyab, Burma, on 18 December 1870; he was brought up in Devon by his aunts after his mother's death, served in the Burma police (1893–95), and worked as a journalist in London and as a foreign correspondent in the Balkans and Russia. Reginald (1904), Reginald in Russia (1910), The Chronicles of Clovis (1911) and Beasts and Super-Beasts (1914) made his name; he enlisted in 1914 at forty-three, refused a commission, and was killed by a sniper at Beaumont-Hamel on 14 November 1916.
literary_profile: Saki is the greatest English writer of the comic short story: his Reginald and Clovis stories are the most perfect examples of the surprise ending in the language, and their satire of Edwardian society — the aunts, the house parties, the hunting, the children — is far more savage than the surface gaiety suggests. 'Sredni Vashtar', 'Tobermory' and 'The Open Window' are permanent anthology pieces, and his death in the war cut off one of the period's most distinctive comic talents.
stylistic_characteristics: The short story built on a single surprise; the epigram and the outrageous aside; the child's revenge on the adult world; the animal as agent of retribution; the comedy of the English house party; the ending that turns the whole story over in a line.
intellectual_concerns: Edwardian society and its aunts; childhood, cruelty and the revenge of the child; the English house party and the hunting field; animals as moral agents; the supernatural played for comedy; the war and the end of the Edwardian idyll.
historical_significance: Saki is the greatest English writer of the comic short story and the finest satirist of Edwardian society: 'Sredni Vashtar', 'Tobermory' and 'The Open Window' are permanent, his surprise endings taught a whole century how a short story works, and his death in the war made him the period's most poignant casualty among the comic writers.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the working-class novel of the Depression and the documentary of the dole
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of Love on the Dole, the most influential English working-class novel of the 1930s.
biography: Born Walter Greenwood in Salford on 17 December 1903, the son of a barber's assistant; he left school at thirteen and worked in a warehouse, a pawnbroker's office and an engineering works before writing Love on the Dole (1933) in the Salford public library while unemployed. The novel was dramatised in 1934 and filmed in 1941, and he remained a professional writer, publishing His Worship the Mayor (1934), Standing Room Only (1936) and the autobiographical There Was a Time (1967). He died at Adlington, Lancashire, on 13 September 1974.
literary_profile: Greenwood wrote the definitive English novel of the Depression: Love on the Dole sold over 70,000 copies in its first year, was banned in some libraries, and became the most performed English play of the thirties. It is the period's clearest literary record of the means test, the dole and the pawnshop, and it made a working-class writer from a Salford warehouse a national figure.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, documentary, unadorned prose; the transcribed Lancashire speech; the working-class family as the unit of the story; the specific detail of wages, rents and the pawnshop; the political argument carried by incident and not by speech.
intellectual_concerns: The Depression and unemployment; the dole, the means test and the pawnshop; the Salford working class and the industrial town; the position of women and the marriage market of poverty; the class solidarity and the betrayal of the Labour movement; respectability and shame.
historical_significance: Greenwood wrote the definitive English novel of the Depression and the most performed English play of the 1930s: Love on the Dole changed the terms in which poverty could be described, gave the working class a literature of its own and remains the period's most direct record of the dole.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the sea novel, the working-class tragedy and the Irish Liverpool
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the great neglected English writer of the sea and the Liverpool Irish poor, and one of the finest prose stylists of the period.
biography: Born James Joseph Hanley in Liverpool on 3 September 1897 to Irish parents; he went to sea at thirteen as a trimmer and a fireman, served in the merchant marine in the First World War, and worked as a railwayman and a ferry hand before writing. Drift (1930), Boy (1931, prosecuted for obscenity), The Furys (1935) and the rest of the five-volume Furys chronicle made his name; he wrote some forty books, and his play Say Nothing (1962) was staged at the Royal Court. He died at Llandudno on 11 November 1985.
literary_profile: Hanley is the great neglected English novelist of the working poor: The Furys sequence is the finest English family novel of the Liverpool Irish poor, Boy is one of the boldest books of the period (prosecuted for obscenity in 1934), and his sea stories stand with Conrad's as the best in the language. His prose — harsh, unadorned, sometimes ungrammatical in its fidelity to speech — is the sound of the working poor of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, harsh, unadorned prose; the transcribed Liverpool Irish speech; the working family as a chronicle across volumes; the ship, the stokehold and the sea; the sexual matter recorded without euphemism; the dialogue that carries the whole story.
intellectual_concerns: The Liverpool Irish poor and the docks; the sea, the ship and the stoker's life; poverty, family and the mother; sexuality and the abuse of the young; the merchant marine in war; emigration and the Irish inheritance.
historical_significance: Hanley is the finest neglected English novelist of the working poor: The Furys is a permanent family chronicle, Boy one of the boldest books of the period, and his sea stories stand with Conrad's. He wrote the Liverpool Irish poor as Dickens wrote London, and his neglect is one of the scandals of English literary history.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the narrative craft and the colonial short story
literary_identity: Novelist, playwright and short-story writer; the most widely read English storyteller of the twentieth century and the master of the plain narrative.
biography: Born William Somerset Maugham at the British embassy in Paris on 25 January 1874; orphaned young, he trained as a doctor at St Thomas's and drew on the slums for Liza of Lambeth (1897). Of Human Bondage (1915), The Moon and Sixpence (1919), the plays that made him rich in the 1900s, Cakes and Ale (1930), The Razor's Edge (1944) and the stories of The Trembling of a Leaf (1921) followed. He worked in intelligence in the First World War and died at Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat on 16 December 1965.
literary_profile: Maugham was the most widely read English storyteller of the twentieth century and the master of the plain narrative: Of Human Bondage gave the English novel its great study of obsession, The Moon and Sixpence and Cakes and Ale its satires of the artist, and the colonial stories of The Trembling of a Leaf created the modern short story of the tropics.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person narrator who listens rather than judges; the plain, unadorned, perfectly paced sentence; the story told at a club or on a verandah; the ironic ending withheld to the last line; the refusal of rhetoric and of experiment.
intellectual_concerns: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist; sexuality, the new psychology; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation.
historical_significance: Maugham was the most widely read English storyteller of the twentieth century: Of Human Bondage is the great English novel of obsession, Cakes and Ale the finest satire of the literary life, and the colonial stories of The Trembling of a Leaf created the modern short story of the tropics and made the plain narrative the dominant English prose style of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-American; the comic invention and the language of the absurd
literary_identity: Humorist and novelist; the creator of Jeeves and Bertie Wooster, and the finest comic prose writer in English.
biography: Born Pelham Grenville Wodehouse at Guildford on 15 October 1881; he worked in a bank and then as a comic writer for the London magazines, creating Psmith in 1903 and publishing My Man Jeeves in 1919. Right Ho, Jeeves (1934), The Code of the Woosters (1938), Blandings Castle (1935) and some ninety books followed. He lived in America from 1914 and died at Southampton, New York, on 14 February 1975.
literary_profile: Wodehouse was the finest comic prose writer in English and the greatest inventor of comic plots of the century: Jeeves and Wooster, Blandings and Psmith gave the language a mythology of its own, and his prose style is the most admired in English comedy since Dickens.
stylistic_characteristics: The elaborate comic plot of farce and coincidence; the invented slang and the classical allusion side by side; the perfectly timed subordinate clause; the running cast of aunts, valets and peers; the refusal of any shadow of real harm.
intellectual_concerns: Class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income; the jazz age and the pleasure economy; the suburb, the villa, and the new domesticity.
historical_significance: P. G. Wodehouse was the finest comic prose writer in English and the greatest inventor of comic plots of the century: Jeeves and Wooster gave the language a mythology of its own, and his prose style is the most admired in English comedy since Dickens.
